hints: Look closely at which atoms the dotted line joins, it should link the O of one water to the H of the other water, not H to H or O to O.
Remember oxygen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so check which end should be slightly negative (delta-) and which end should be slightly positive (delta+) in each diagram.
walkthrough:
**Recall why water is polar**

Water is a polar molecule because oxygen pulls shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen.

That gives us this rule:
$$O = \delta- \text{ (slightly negative), } H = \delta+ \text{ (slightly positive)}$$

**Recall where a hydrogen bond forms**

A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between a lone pair on one oxygen and a hydrogen already bonded to another oxygen.

So the dotted line must go: O...H, with opposite partial charges attracting.

**Check the diagrams and choose**

Only B shows O(delta-)...H(delta+) with correct partial charges on all atoms.

The others either use full charges or swap delta+ and delta- around, so B is the winner.

options.A: Shows the correct O...H position but uses full + and - charges. Water only has partial charges, delta+ and delta-, not full ions.
options.B: Correctly shows O(delta-) of one molecule attracting H(delta+) of the other, with all O as delta- and all H as delta+.
options.C: Has the charges backwards, showing H as delta- and O as delta+. This is opposite to real electronegativity in water.
options.D: Has charges backwards and uses full charges. O should be delta-, not +, and H should be delta+, not -.
